newsitem.title: USA: US cities rebounding but face big hurdles - Clinton.
newsitem.headline: US cities rebounding but face big hurdles - Clinton.

text.p: U.S. cities are rebounding from decades of decline but still face major hurdles to reduce poverty, create jobs and attract middle class residents, according to a report released Monday by President Clinton.

"America cannot afford to be divided into two nations -- one doing well in the suburbs, and the other marginalized in urban neighborhoods," concludes the report organized by Housing and Urban Development Secretary Andrew Cuomo and released at a U.S. Conference of Mayors meeting here.
Vice President Al Gore called the document "the most significant report on the condition of urban America in a generation."
The report, entitled "State of the Cities," says urban American faces three major challenges:
* Most new jobs are being created in suburbs rather than cities, and large cities actually lost jobs in the early 1990s;
* American's poor have grown more socially and economically isolated and more physically concentrated in central cities over the past two decades.
Specifically, the poverty rate in cities rose from 14.2 percent in 1970 to 21.5 percent in 1993, then dropped slightly to 20.6 percent in 1995, the report says.
Also, the concentration of the poor in cities is increasing, with over 10 percent of city residents living in census tracts with a poverty rate of 40 percent or more, the report says;

* Finally, the long-term migration of the middle class from cities to suburbs continues in the 1990s, with only 11 of 30 largest cities in 1970 having more people today than two decades ago, the report says.

Clinton said his second-term urban agenda will focus on seven steps to address the problems, including increasing homeownership in cities, passing a second round of Empowerment Zones and Enterprise Communities, and cleaning up urban "brownfields." Brownfields are contaminated former industrial sites.

Clinton said he also will focus on ensuring better and more affordable housing, increasing opportunities for welfare recipients moving into the world of work, fighting crime in urban neighborhoods; and increasing education opportunities for all Americans.
